sections.heading: Urinary tract infection: organisms, virulence and the level of infection
sections.html:
Most urinary tract infections (UTIs) are ascending: bowel flora colonise the periurethral area, enter the bladder through the urethra and can climb the ureter to the renal pelvis. Women are affected far more often because the urethra is short and close to the anus. Hematogenous seeding of the kidney is uncommon and points to Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia or candidemia.

Host factors

  • Urine flow is the main defence. Anything that causes stasis raises the risk: obstruction (stone, prostate enlargement, pregnancy-related ureteral dilation), neurogenic bladder, vesicoureteral reflux.
  • Foreign bodies: catheters carry biofilm, which protects organisms from antibiotics and host defences.
  • Sexual activity, spermicides and diaphragms change periurethral flora and inoculate the bladder.
  • Low estrogen after menopause lets vaginal lactobacilli fall and uropathogens colonise.
  • Diabetes: glycosuria, impaired neutrophil function and autonomic bladder dysfunction.

Organisms

OrganismSettingClue on the exam
Escherichia coliAbout three quarters of community UTIsLactose fermenter; P fimbriae bind uroepithelial glycolipids and favour pyelonephritis; type 1 fimbriae favour cystitis
Staphylococcus saprophyticusYoung, sexually active womenGram-positive cocci in clusters, coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant
Proteus mirabilisRecurrent or catheter UTI, stonesUrease splits urea to ammonia, alkaline urine (pH often above 7.5), struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate) staghorn calculi; swarming motility
Klebsiella pneumoniaeHospital, diabetes, alcohol useMucoid, encapsulated lactose fermenter; urease positive
Enterococcus speciesCatheters, instrumentation, older menGram-positive cocci in chains; intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins
Pseudomonas aeruginosaCatheters, recent hospital careNon-lactose fermenter, oxidase positive, grape-like odour, blue-green pigment

Urinalysis

Leukocyte esterase marks neutrophils (pyuria). The nitrite test turns positive when Enterobacterales reduce dietary nitrate to nitrite; it is often negative with Enterococcus and S. saprophyticus, which do not reduce nitrate, and when urine has sat in the bladder only briefly. White blood cell casts form only in renal tubules, so they place the infection (or inflammation) in the kidney.

[[figure:s23c-fig110101-1]]

Pathology of acute pyelonephritis

Grossly, the kidney is swollen with yellow cortical abscesses. Microscopically, neutrophils fill tubules and the interstitium while glomeruli are relatively spared. Complications include renal or perinephric abscess, papillary necrosis (diabetes, obstruction, sickle cell disease, analgesic use) and, in diabetes, emphysematous pyelonephritis with gas in the parenchyma.

Exam trap: casts mean kidney. Pyuria with bacteria but no casts fits cystitis; pyuria with white cell casts and fever fits pyelonephritis (or, without bacteria, interstitial nephritis).

Chronic and unusual infections

  • Chronic pyelonephritis: recurrent infection on a background of reflux or obstruction gives coarse, asymmetric corticomedullary scars over blunted calyces, most marked at the poles. Tubules fill with eosinophilic casts that resemble thyroid follicles ("thyroidization").
  • Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis: a destructive chronic infection, usually with an obstructing staghorn stone and Proteus or E. coli. Lipid-laden foamy macrophages form yellow masses that can mimic renal cell carcinoma; treatment is usually nephrectomy.
  • Genitourinary tuberculosis: hematogenous spread, often years after the primary infection. Classic clue: sterile pyuria (white cells, routine culture negative) with hematuria; caseating granulomas, calyceal distortion, ureteral strictures. Diagnose with acid-fast culture or nucleic acid testing of several first-morning urine samples.
  • Schistosoma haematobium: freshwater exposure in Africa or the Middle East; adult worms live in the vesical venous plexus, and eggs with a terminal spine lodge in the bladder wall. Terminal hematuria, granulomatous fibrosis, obstructive uropathy and, long term, squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Treatment: praziquantel.
  • BK polyomavirus: reactivates in kidney transplant recipients on strong immunosuppression and causes tubulointerstitial nephritis with intranuclear inclusions ("decoy cells" in urine) and graft dysfunction. The main step is to reduce immunosuppression.
  • Adenovirus: hemorrhagic cystitis in children and transplant recipients.

Memory aid (Naadi): "Stones that smell of ammonia": urease producers (Proteus, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Ureaplasma) make urine alkaline and build struvite.

sections.heading: Urinary tract infection: diagnosis and management
sections.html:
Classify first

Management depends on where the infection is and who has it.

  • Acute uncomplicated cystitis: a healthy, nonpregnant, premenopausal or postmenopausal woman with dysuria, frequency and urgency, and no fever, flank pain or systemic signs.
  • Complicated UTI: infection beyond the bladder (fever, flank pain, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) or infection in a patient with features that predict failure: pregnancy, male sex, catheter, obstruction or stones, urologic abnormality, kidney transplant or significant immunocompromise.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria: bacteria in a properly collected urine without symptoms of UTI.

Uncomplicated cystitis

A typical history is enough; a dipstick helps when the story is unclear. Urine culture is not needed for a first, typical episode, but is obtained for recurrence, failure, atypical symptoms or any complicated feature. First-line choices:

DrugUsual courseAvoid or limit when
Nitrofurantoin5 dayseGFR below about 30 mL/min/1.73 m², suspected pyelonephritis (inadequate tissue levels)
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole3 daysLocal resistance above about 20%, use in the past 3 months, sulfa allergy
FosfomycinSingle doseSlightly less effective; not for pyelonephritis
Pivmecillinam3–5 daysPenicillin allergy

Fluoroquinolones and beta-lactams are second line for cystitis: they work, but fluoroquinolones carry tendon, aortic, neurologic and C. difficile risks, and short beta-lactam courses fail more often.

Pyelonephritis

  • Obtain a urinalysis and a urine culture before antibiotics in every case; blood cultures if septic or admitted.
  • Outpatient (stable, able to take oral fluids): an oral fluoroquinolone for 5–7 days, or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 7–14 days when the isolate is susceptible. Where fluoroquinolone resistance is common, give one initial parenteral dose of a long-acting agent such as ceftriaxone.
  • Admit for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy, suspected obstruction or failure of oral therapy; start an IV agent such as ceftriaxone, broadened (for example to piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem) when there is septic shock or risk of resistant organisms.
  • Imaging (CT abdomen and pelvis, or ultrasound when contrast or radiation should be avoided) is for severe illness, suspected stone or obstruction, or no improvement after 48–72 hours. It finds abscess, obstruction and emphysematous pyelonephritis.
  • Infected obstructed kidney is a urologic emergency: antibiotics alone fail, so decompress urgently with a ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy. Stone removal waits until the infection clears.
  • Emphysematous pyelonephritis (gas in the renal parenchyma, nearly always in diabetes): IV antibiotics with percutaneous drainage; nephrectomy if that fails.

Special populations

  • Pregnancy: screen once with a urine culture early in pregnancy (around 12–16 weeks) and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria, because untreated bacteriuria leads to pyelonephritis and preterm birth. Safe choices include cephalexin, amoxicillin-clavulanate, fosfomycin and nitrofurantoin (avoid nitrofurantoin near term and, if alternatives exist, in the first trimester; avoid trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in the first trimester and near term; avoid fluoroquinolones and tetracyclines). Pyelonephritis in pregnancy is treated in hospital with IV beta-lactam therapy, and many clinicians then give suppressive therapy for the rest of the pregnancy.
  • Asymptomatic bacteriuria outside pregnancy is not screened for or treated, including in older adults, people with diabetes, spinal cord injury or long-term catheters. The other exception is a planned urologic procedure that breaches the mucosa (for example transurethral resection of the prostate).
  • Men: every UTI is treated as complicated; treat for about 7 days, longer (up to 14 days) if prostatitis is suspected or response is slow.
  • Catheter-associated UTI: diagnose only with symptoms (fever, suprapubic or flank pain, delirium without another cause). Remove the catheter if possible, or replace a catheter that has been in place for more than about 2 weeks, and send culture from the new catheter before antibiotics.
  • Recurrent UTI (2 or more in 6 months or 3 or more in a year): confirm each episode with culture. Options are behavioural measures, vaginal estrogen in postmenopausal women, post-coital or continuous low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis, and patient-started treatment. Image the tract only if there are atypical features (for example, recurrence with Proteus, hematuria between infections, or a man).

Exam trap: a confused nursing-home resident with a positive urine culture and no urinary symptoms or fever does not have a UTI. Look for another cause and do not treat the bacteriuria.

figures.caption: Figure. Urinary tract infection by level. Most infections ascend from the urethra; fever, flank pain and white blood cell casts place the infection in the kidney.

sets.title: Fever and flank pain in pregnancy

items.stemHtml: A 20-year-old woman has had burning on urination and urinary frequency for 2 days. She became sexually active with a new partner 3 weeks ago. Temperature is 36.9°C (98.4°F), and there is mild suprapubic tenderness without flank tenderness. Urinalysis shows leukocyte esterase and many white blood cells; the nitrite test is negative. Urine culture grows gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase positive, coagulase negative and grow normally around a novobiocin disk. Which of the following is the most likely organism?
items.explanationHtml:
Catalase-positive, coagulase-negative staphylococci that are resistant to novobiocin (they grow up to the disk) are S. saprophyticus, the second most common cause of cystitis in young, sexually active women. It does not reduce nitrate, so the nitrite test is often negative.

Takeaway: coagulase-negative staphylococcal cystitis in a young sexually active woman with novobiocin resistance is S. saprophyticus.

whyNot.A: Enterococci are catalase negative and grow in chains or pairs, not clusters.
whyNot.B: S. aureus is coagulase positive; in urine it usually signals bacteremia seeding the kidney.
whyNot.C: S. epidermidis is also coagulase negative, but it is novobiocin sensitive and causes catheter or device infections rather than cystitis in healthy women.
whyNot.E: Group B streptococci are catalase negative and form chains; they cause bacteriuria mainly in pregnancy and older adults with diabetes.

items.objective: Identify Staphylococcus saprophyticus from its setting and laboratory features (coagulase negative, novobiocin resistant).

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has fever of 39.2°C (102.6°F), chills and right flank pain 4 days after symptoms of cystitis began. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine culture grows a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod. Molecular typing of the isolate shows a gene encoding an adhesin that binds galactose-containing glycolipids on uroepithelial cells of the renal pelvis. Which of the following virulence factors does this gene encode?
items.explanationHtml:
The patient has acute pyelonephritis due to uropathogenic E. coli. P (pyelonephritis-associated) fimbriae bind the galactose-containing P blood-group glycolipids on uroepithelium, letting the organism resist urine flow and ascend to the kidney. Type 1 fimbriae, which bind mannose, matter more for bladder colonisation.

Takeaway: P fimbriae are the E. coli adhesin most linked to ascending pyelonephritis.

whyNot.A: The K1 capsule protects E. coli from phagocytosis and complement and is the key factor in neonatal meningitis; it is not an adhesin.
whyNot.C: Shiga-like toxin is made by enterohemorrhagic E. coli and causes bloody diarrhea and hemolytic uremic syndrome.
whyNot.D: Heat-labile toxin is the enterotoxigenic E. coli toxin of traveler's diarrhea; it raises cAMP in enterocytes.
whyNot.E: Lipid A drives septic shock through TLR4 signalling but does not mediate attachment to uroepithelium.

items.objective: Link P fimbriae of uropathogenic E. coli to ascending pyelonephritis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with a long-term indwelling urethral catheter after spinal cord injury has had three urinary tract infections in a year. Urine pH is 8.5. Abdominal radiography shows a large branching radiopaque calculus filling the left renal pelvis and calyces. Urine culture grows a gram-negative rod that spreads in waves across the agar plate. Which of the following enzymes produced by this organism is most responsible for the calculus?
items.explanationHtml:
A swarming gram-negative rod in a catheterised patient is Proteus mirabilis. Its urease splits urea into ammonia and carbon dioxide; ammonia makes urine strongly alkaline, and in alkaline urine magnesium, ammonium and phosphate precipitate as struvite, which can grow into a staghorn calculus. The stone shelters bacteria, so infection recurs until the stone is removed.

Takeaway: alkaline urine plus a staghorn calculus means a urease-producing organism and struvite.

whyNot.A: Beta-lactamase gives antibiotic resistance but does not change urine chemistry or form stones.
whyNot.B: Catalase protects bacteria from hydrogen peroxide; it has no role in stone formation.
whyNot.C: Coagulase is a Staphylococcus aureus enzyme that converts fibrinogen to fibrin.
whyNot.D: Nitrate reductase gives a positive urine nitrite test but does not alkalinise urine.

items.objective: Explain how urease-producing organisms such as Proteus cause struvite staghorn calculi.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, chills, nausea and left flank pain. Temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). There is left costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following findings on urine microscopy most specifically shows that the infection involves the kidney rather than only the bladder?

options.label: A
options.html: Bacteria seen on an unspun specimen

options.label: B
options.html: More than 10 white blood cells per high-power field

options.label: C
options.html: Red blood cells with a normal shape

items.explanationHtml:
Casts are moulds of the tubular lumen made of Tamm-Horsfall glycoprotein. White blood cell casts therefore form only when neutrophils are inside renal tubules, which places the inflammation in the kidney (pyelonephritis or interstitial nephritis). Pyuria, bacteriuria and hematuria occur with cystitis as well.

Takeaway: white blood cell casts localise a UTI to the kidney.

whyNot.A: Bacteriuria occurs with infection at any level of the urinary tract and with contamination.
whyNot.B: Pyuria shows inflammation somewhere in the urinary tract but does not tell bladder from kidney.
whyNot.C: Normally shaped red cells suggest bleeding below the glomerulus, which occurs with hemorrhagic cystitis too.
whyNot.D: Squamous cells mean the specimen is contaminated by vaginal or skin cells.

items.objective: Use white blood cell casts to localise urinary infection to the kidney.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old man who moved from a rural region abroad 10 years ago has had painless intermittent hematuria and urinary frequency for 4 months. He has lost 3 kg. Urinalysis shows many white blood cells and red blood cells on repeated samples, but routine bacterial urine cultures are negative three times. He has not taken antibiotics. Intravenous urography shows irregular, moth-eaten calyces in the right kidney and a narrowed right ureter. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Acid-fast culture and nucleic acid testing of first-morning urine samples

options.label: B
options.html: Serum antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibody titres

options.label: C
options.html: Microscopy of a midday urine sample for eggs with a terminal spine

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat bacterial urine culture on chocolate agar in carbon dioxide

options.label: E
options.html: Urine eosinophil count using a Hansel stain

items.explanationHtml:
Sterile pyuria with hematuria, calyceal destruction and ureteral stricture is the picture of genitourinary tuberculosis, which reaches the kidney by hematogenous spread, often many years after primary infection. Bacilli are shed intermittently, so several first-morning urine samples are sent for mycobacterial culture and nucleic acid testing. Caseating granulomas are seen if tissue is obtained.

Takeaway: sterile pyuria plus hematuria and a deformed collecting system points to renal tuberculosis.

whyNot.B: Lupus nephritis causes active sediment with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts, not calyceal destruction or ureteral strictures.
whyNot.C: Schistosoma haematobium eggs cause terminal hematuria with bladder-wall granulomas and calcification; the infection centres on the bladder, not on destruction of the renal calyces with sterile pyuria.
whyNot.D: Fastidious organisms such as Haemophilus would not produce this destructive chronic picture.
whyNot.E: Urine eosinophils are a weak test for drug-induced interstitial nephritis, which does not deform the calyces.

items.objective: Recognise genitourinary tuberculosis as a cause of sterile pyuria and choose mycobacterial urine testing.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man who grew up farming irrigated land along a river in North Africa has painless gross hematuria. Cystoscopy shows a fungating mass on the posterior bladder wall surrounded by thickened, calcified mucosa. Biopsy of the surrounding wall shows granulomas around calcified ova that carry a terminal spine. Which of the following is the most likely histologic type of the bladder mass?
items.explanationHtml:
Eggs with a terminal spine in the bladder wall are Schistosoma haematobium. Chronic egg-driven inflammation causes squamous metaplasia of the urothelium, and the cancer that follows is typically squamous cell carcinoma. Other chronic irritants (long-term catheters, stones) do the same.

Takeaway: chronic bladder irritation, classically schistosomiasis, leads to squamous metaplasia and squamous cell carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Bladder adenocarcinoma arises mainly from a urachal remnant at the dome or with bladder exstrophy.
whyNot.B: Clear cell carcinoma is the common renal cortical cancer, not a bladder tumour linked to parasites.
whyNot.C: Small cell carcinoma of the bladder is rare and is not linked to schistosomiasis.
whyNot.E: Urothelial carcinoma is the commonest bladder cancer overall, linked to smoking and aromatic amines, but chronic schistosomal inflammation shifts the type to squamous.

items.objective: Associate Schistosoma haematobium infection with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman has 3 months of malaise, low-grade fever, left flank pain and a 6-kg weight loss. She has had recurrent urinary infections with Proteus mirabilis. CT shows an enlarged, nonfunctioning left kidney containing a staghorn calculus and several low-density masses replacing the parenchyma. Nephrectomy is performed. Microscopy of the yellow masses shows sheets of macrophages with abundant foamy cytoplasm mixed with plasma cells and neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: C
options.html: Renal malakoplakia confined to the bladder

items.explanationHtml:
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a destructive chronic infection of an obstructed kidney, usually with a staghorn stone and Proteus or E. coli. Lipid-laden (foamy) macrophages form yellow nodules that can look like a tumour on imaging and grossly. The kidney is usually nonfunctioning, and nephrectomy is the usual treatment.

Takeaway: staghorn stone, chronic infection and foamy macrophages replacing the kidney is xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.

whyNot.A: Angiomyolipoma contains fat, smooth muscle and thick-walled vessels; it is a benign tumour, often with tuberous sclerosis, not an infection.
whyNot.B: Clear cell carcinoma cells contain glycogen and lipid, but they are malignant epithelial cells in nests with delicate vessels, not macrophages with plasma cells and neutrophils.
whyNot.C: Malakoplakia shows macrophages with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies (calcified inclusions) and usually involves the bladder; it does not explain the replaced kidney and staghorn stone.
whyNot.D: Renal tuberculosis forms caseating granulomas with epithelioid macrophages, and routine cultures are negative.

items.objective: Recognise xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis from its setting and histology.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman received a kidney transplant 9 months ago and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. Her serum creatinine has risen from 1.2 to 2.1 mg/dL over 6 weeks. She feels well. Urine cytology shows tubular epithelial cells with enlarged nuclei containing homogeneous basophilic inclusions. Allograft biopsy shows tubulointerstitial inflammation and the same intranuclear inclusions, which stain for SV40 large T antigen. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
items.explanationHtml:
Intranuclear inclusions in tubular cells ("decoy cells" in urine) staining for SV40 antigen mean BK polyomavirus nephropathy, which reactivates when immunosuppression is intense. No antiviral is reliably effective, so the core step is to reduce immunosuppression (typically lowering or stopping the antimetabolite and lowering the calcineurin inhibitor) while watching for rejection.

Takeaway: BK virus nephropathy in a kidney graft is treated by reducing immunosuppression.

whyNot.A: Ganciclovir treats cytomegalovirus; it has no meaningful activity against BK polyomavirus.
whyNot.B: More calcineurin inhibitor would deepen immunosuppression and allow more viral replication.
whyNot.D: Pulse steroids treat acute cellular rejection; giving them for BK nephropathy would worsen the infection.
whyNot.E: Acyclovir is for herpes simplex and varicella zoster and does not act on polyomaviruses.

items.objective: Recognise BK polyomavirus nephropathy in a kidney transplant recipient and reduce immunosuppression.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has had dysuria, urinary frequency and urgency for 1 day. She has no fever, flank pain or vaginal discharge, and she is not pregnant (urine hCG negative). She has had no antibiotics in the past year and no drug allergies. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). There is mild suprapubic tenderness and no costovertebral angle tenderness. Urine dipstick is positive for leukocyte esterase and nitrite. Her eGFR is above 90 mL/min/1.73 m². Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: C
options.html: Pelvic examination with nucleic acid testing before any treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Urine culture, with antibiotics only if the culture is positive

items.explanationHtml:
This is acute uncomplicated cystitis: a healthy, nonpregnant woman with typical lower-tract symptoms, no fever or flank pain and no complicating features. A first-line agent such as nitrofurantoin for 5 days (or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 3 days where resistance is low, or single-dose fosfomycin) is appropriate without a culture.

Takeaway: treat typical uncomplicated cystitis empirically with a first-line agent; culture is for complicated, recurrent or atypical cases.

whyNot.B: Fluoroquinolones work but are reserved for pyelonephritis or when first-line agents cannot be used, because of adverse effects and resistance.
whyNot.C: Without vaginal discharge or irritation, sexually transmitted urethritis or vaginitis is unlikely, and treatment need not wait.
whyNot.D: Imaging has no role in a first episode of uncomplicated cystitis.
whyNot.E: Culture is unnecessary for a first typical episode, and waiting 2 days for it delays relief.

items.objective: Treat acute uncomplicated cystitis empirically with a first-line agent.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 13 weeks' gestation comes for a routine prenatal visit. She has no urinary symptoms. A screening urine culture grows more than 100,000 colony-forming units/mL of Escherichia coli, susceptible to cephalexin, nitrofurantoin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. She has no allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: No treatment, because she has no symptoms

options.label: B
options.html: Oral cephalexin for 5–7 days, then a follow-up urine culture

options.label: E
options.html: Repeat the urine culture at 28 weeks' gestation

items.explanationHtml:
In pregnancy, asymptomatic bacteriuria is treated, because about a third of untreated women develop pyelonephritis, which is linked to preterm birth and low birth weight. A short course of a pregnancy-safe agent guided by susceptibility, such as cephalexin, is appropriate, followed by a test-of-cure culture and periodic rescreening.

Takeaway: screen once early in pregnancy and treat asymptomatic bacteriuria with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic.

whyNot.A: Pregnancy is the main exception to the rule of not treating asymptomatic bacteriuria.
whyNot.C: Fluoroquinolones are generally avoided in pregnancy when safer options exist.
whyNot.D: Tetracyclines are contraindicated in pregnancy (fetal tooth discoloration and bone effects).
whyNot.E: Waiting leaves her at risk of pyelonephritis in the meantime.

items.objective: Treat asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy with a pregnancy-safe antibiotic.

items.stemHtml: An 84-year-old woman who lives in a nursing home and has moderate dementia is evaluated because a urine culture, sent after staff noticed her urine was cloudy and malodorous, grew more than 100,000 colony-forming units/mL of Klebsiella pneumoniae. She has no fever, change in mental status, dysuria, new incontinence or abdominal pain. Vital signs are normal. Examination shows no suprapubic or costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Oral antibiotic for 7 days based on susceptibilities

items.explanationHtml:
This is asymptomatic bacteriuria, which is common in older adults, especially in long-term care. Cloudy or smelly urine is not a symptom of infection. Treatment does not reduce symptomatic infection or mortality and does cause adverse drug events, C. difficile infection and resistant organisms, so the right step is no antibiotics.

Takeaway: outside pregnancy and planned urologic procedures, do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria.

whyNot.A: Prophylaxis is for recurrent symptomatic UTI, not bacteriuria without symptoms.
whyNot.C: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults gives harm without benefit.
whyNot.D: Routine surveillance cultures lead to unnecessary treatment.
whyNot.E: Even a single dose is unnecessary and selects for resistance.

items.objective: Avoid treating asymptomatic bacteriuria in older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has 2 days of fever, chills, nausea and right flank pain. She is not pregnant. She vomited once yesterday but has kept down fluids and food today. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F), pulse 98/min and blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows pyuria, bacteriuria and white blood cell casts. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Local fluoroquinolone resistance among E. coli is below 10%. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the abdomen and pelvis before any antibiotic

options.label: E
options.html: Urine culture, then oral ciprofloxacin for 7 days

items.explanationHtml:
She has acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis and is stable and able to take oral fluids, so outpatient treatment is appropriate. Send a urine culture before antibiotics, then give an oral fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin for 7 days, or levofloxacin for 5 days) where local resistance is low, and adjust to susceptibilities.

Takeaway: stable pyelonephritis: culture, then an oral fluoroquinolone (or susceptible trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole); admit only for sepsis, vomiting, pregnancy or obstruction.

whyNot.A: Imaging is for severe illness, suspected obstruction or no response after 48–72 hours, and it should not delay antibiotics.
whyNot.B: She is not septic and can take oral drugs; a carbapenem would be broader than needed.
whyNot.C: Nitrofurantoin does not reach adequate kidney tissue levels and should not be used for pyelonephritis.
whyNot.D: Fosfomycin as a single dose is for cystitis and is not adequate for pyelonephritis.

items.objective: Manage stable acute pyelonephritis with a urine culture and an oral agent that reaches renal tissue.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man has 1 day of severe left flank pain radiating to the groin, followed by fever and rigors. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F), pulse 118/min and blood pressure 96/58 mm Hg after 2 L of intravenous crystalloid. There is left costovertebral angle tenderness. Leukocyte count is 19,500/mm³ and serum creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Blood and urine cultures are drawn, and intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam is started. Noncontrast CT shows a 7-mm stone in the proximal left ureter with moderate hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue antibiotics and wait for spontaneous stone passage

options.label: C
options.html: Start tamsulosin and discharge with oral antibiotics

options.label: D
options.html: Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy and stone extraction today

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent decompression with a ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy

items.explanationHtml:
An infected, obstructed kidney with sepsis is a urologic emergency. Antibiotics cannot sterilise a closed, pressurised collecting system, so the kidney must be decompressed urgently, by retrograde ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy, alongside antibiotics and resuscitation. Definitive stone treatment is delayed until the infection has resolved.

Takeaway: stone plus obstruction plus infection means drain first, treat the stone later.

whyNot.A: Waiting with an obstructed, infected kidney risks worsening septic shock and loss of the kidney.
whyNot.B: Shock wave lithotripsy in active infection can worsen sepsis, and it does not drain the system quickly.
whyNot.C: Medical expulsive therapy is for uncomplicated stones without infection; he is septic and needs admission.
whyNot.D: Definitive stone surgery during sepsis raises the risk of bacteremia; drainage alone is the safer first step.

items.objective: Decompress an obstructed, infected kidney urgently before definitive stone treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (hemoglobin A1c 10.8%) has had 4 days of fever, right flank pain and vomiting. Temperature is 39.0°C (102.2°F), pulse 112/min and blood pressure 104/64 mm Hg. Serum glucose is 386 mg/dL and creatinine 1.9 mg/dL. Urine culture is pending. Intravenous ceftriaxone and fluids are started. CT of the abdomen shows gas within the right renal parenchyma extending into the perirenal space, without a ureteral stone or hydronephrosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step, in addition to antibiotics and glucose control?

options.label: C
options.html: No intervention; continue intravenous antibiotics alone for 6 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Percutaneous catheter drainage of the right kidney

items.explanationHtml:
Gas in the renal parenchyma in a patient with diabetes is emphysematous pyelonephritis, a necrotising infection usually caused by E. coli or Klebsiella. When gas extends beyond the parenchyma, antibiotics alone have high mortality; the standard is antibiotics with percutaneous drainage, with emergency nephrectomy if she does not improve or has extensive disease with shock.

Takeaway: emphysematous pyelonephritis needs source control (percutaneous drainage, or nephrectomy) plus antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Retrograde pyelography evaluates the collecting system; there is no obstruction, and it would not drain parenchymal gas.
whyNot.B: Hyperbaric oxygen is not a standard treatment for this condition and would delay source control.
whyNot.C: Antibiotics alone are reserved for gas limited to the collecting system; extension beyond the kidney needs drainage.
whyNot.E: Waiting a week in a septic patient with a necrotising infection is unsafe.

items.objective: Recognise emphysematous pyelonephritis and arrange source control.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman has had four culture-confirmed episodes of acute cystitis in the past 12 months, each with E. coli and each resolving with a short course of nitrofurantoin. Between episodes she is well, and urinalysis between episodes shows no blood. Post-void residual volume is 30 mL. Pelvic examination shows pale, thin vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae; there is no prolapse. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to reduce recurrences?
items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent uncomplicated cystitis in a postmenopausal woman with genitourinary atrophy is driven partly by low estrogen, which lets lactobacilli fall and uropathogens colonise. Vaginal estrogen restores the vaginal flora and reduces recurrences, with minimal systemic absorption. Low-dose antibiotic prophylaxis is an alternative if this fails, using a first-line agent rather than a fluoroquinolone.

Takeaway: for recurrent UTI after menopause with atrophy, start vaginal estrogen.

whyNot.A: Upper-tract imaging is not needed for recurrent uncomplicated cystitis without hematuria, stones, Proteus or other atypical features.
whyNot.B: Cystoscopy is not indicated without hematuria or another atypical feature.
whyNot.C: Fluoroquinolones are a poor choice for long-term prophylaxis because of adverse effects and resistance.
whyNot.D: Systemic hormone therapy does not reduce UTIs and carries cardiovascular and breast risks.

items.objective: Prevent recurrent UTI in a postmenopausal woman with vaginal estrogen.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man has had an indwelling urethral catheter for 5 weeks because of urinary retention after a stroke. Today he has a temperature of 38.7°C (101.7°F), new confusion and suprapubic discomfort. Blood pressure is 128/74 mm Hg. There is no cough, diarrhea or wound. Urinalysis from the catheter bag shows pyuria and bacteriuria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step before starting antibiotics?

options.label: A
options.html: Collect urine from the drainage bag for culture

options.label: B
options.html: Irrigate the existing catheter with saline

options.label: C
options.html: Replace the catheter and send a urine culture from the new catheter

items.explanationHtml:
He has a symptomatic catheter-associated UTI. A catheter in place for more than about 2 weeks is coated with biofilm; cultures from it reflect colonisation, and the biofilm protects organisms from antibiotics. The catheter should be removed or replaced, and urine for culture collected from the fresh catheter before antibiotics start. Then reassess whether he still needs a catheter at all (intermittent catheterisation may be possible).

Takeaway: in catheter-associated UTI, replace a long-dwelling catheter and culture from the new one before antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Bag urine is contaminated and overgrown; it should never be used for culture.
whyNot.B: Irrigation does not clear biofilm infection and is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Imaging is not routine unless there is suspected obstruction, poor response or severe sepsis.
whyNot.E: Bladder irrigation with antibiotics is not effective treatment for catheter-associated UTI.

items.objective: Manage catheter-associated UTI by replacing the catheter and culturing from the new one.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, at 22 weeks' gestation has had fever, chills and right flank pain for 1 day. She vomited three times today. Temperature is 39.1°C (102.4°F), pulse 108/min and blood pressure 108/66 mm Hg. Fetal heart rate is 160/min. There is right costovertebral angle tenderness. Urinalysis shows pyuria, bacteriuria and white blood cell casts. Urine and blood cultures are sent. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: Discharge with oral amoxicillin for 3 days

options.label: D
options.html: Discharge with oral nitrofurantoin for 7 days

options.label: E
options.html: Observe without antibiotics until culture results return

items.explanationHtml:
Pyelonephritis in pregnancy carries risks of sepsis, acute respiratory distress syndrome and preterm labour, so it is treated in hospital with an intravenous beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone, adjusted to culture results and switched to oral therapy once she has been afebrile for 24–48 hours.

Takeaway: pyelonephritis in pregnancy means admission and IV beta-lactam therapy.

whyNot.B: Fluoroquinolones are avoided in pregnancy when safer agents exist.
whyNot.C: Oral amoxicillin has poor activity against many E. coli strains, and 3 days is far too short for pyelonephritis.
whyNot.D: Nitrofurantoin does not achieve kidney tissue levels and cannot treat pyelonephritis; she is also vomiting.
whyNot.E: Withholding antibiotics in a febrile pregnant patient with pyelonephritis risks sepsis and preterm labour.

items.objective: Admit and treat pyelonephritis in pregnancy with an intravenous beta-lactam.

items.stemHtml: The patient was admitted and treated with intravenous ceftriaxone. Urine culture grew pan-sensitive E. coli. She became afebrile after 36 hours, was switched to oral cephalexin and completed a 14-day course. She is now at 25 weeks' gestation, feels well, and a repeat urine culture is negative. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step for the rest of her pregnancy?

options.label: A
options.html: Low-dose daily antibiotic suppression until delivery

options.label: B
options.html: No further urine cultures unless symptoms recur

options.label: C
options.html: Renal ultrasonography every 4 weeks until delivery

options.label: D
options.html: A repeat 14-day course of cephalexin each trimester

items.explanationHtml:
Pyelonephritis recurs in a meaningful share of pregnant women. A common approach is low-dose suppressive antibiotic therapy (for example nitrofurantoin or cephalexin at bedtime) for the rest of the pregnancy, with periodic urine cultures; close surveillance with repeat cultures is an accepted alternative.

Takeaway: after pyelonephritis in pregnancy, prevent recurrence with suppression or close culture surveillance until delivery.

whyNot.B: Waiting for symptoms misses recurrent bacteriuria, which can progress to another pyelonephritis.
whyNot.C: Serial imaging does not prevent recurrence; mild dilation of the right collecting system is normal in pregnancy.
whyNot.D: Repeated full treatment courses expose her to more antibiotic than low-dose suppression without added benefit.
whyNot.E: Weekly parenteral antibiotics are not a standard or practical suppression strategy.

items.objective: Prevent recurrent pyelonephritis in pregnancy with suppression or culture surveillance.

cards.frontHtml: Coagulase-negative staphylococcus, novobiocin resistant, causing cystitis in a young sexually active woman?
Which E. coli adhesin is most linked to ascending pyelonephritis?
cards.backHtml: P fimbriae (bind galactose-containing glycolipids on uroepithelium). Type 1 (mannose-binding) fimbriae favour bladder colonisation.

cards.frontHtml: Alkaline urine (pH above 7.5) and a staghorn calculus suggest what kind of organism and stone?
cards.backHtml: A urease producer (classically Proteus mirabilis) and struvite: magnesium ammonium phosphate.

cards.frontHtml: Which urine microscopy finding places an infection in the kidney rather than the bladder?
cards.backHtml: White blood cell casts: casts form only in renal tubules.

cards.frontHtml: Sterile pyuria with hematuria and moth-eaten calyces: likely diagnosis and test?
cards.backHtml: Genitourinary tuberculosis; acid-fast culture and nucleic acid testing of several first-morning urine samples.

cards.frontHtml: Bladder cancer type after chronic Schistosoma haematobium infection?
cards.backHtml: Squamous cell carcinoma (after squamous metaplasia). Treat the infection with praziquantel.

cards.frontHtml: Staghorn stone, nonfunctioning kidney and foamy lipid-laden macrophages that mimic a tumour?
cards.backHtml: Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis (Proteus or E. coli); usually nephrectomy.

cards.frontHtml: Kidney transplant recipient, rising creatinine, urine "decoy cells" with intranuclear inclusions: cause and first step?
First-line options for acute uncomplicated cystitis in a nonpregnant woman?
cards.backHtml: Nitrofurantoin 5 days; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 3 days (if resistance below about 20%); single-dose fosfomycin; pivmecillinam. No culture needed for a first typical episode.

cards.frontHtml: Why is nitrofurantoin wrong for pyelonephritis?
cards.backHtml: It concentrates in urine but does not reach adequate kidney tissue or blood levels.
Pregnancy (screen once early with culture) and before a urologic procedure that breaches the mucosa. Not in older adults, diabetes or catheters.

cards.frontHtml: Septic patient with an obstructing ureteral stone and infected urine: next step after antibiotics?
cards.backHtml: Urgent decompression (ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy); definitive stone treatment later.

cards.frontHtml: Gas in the renal parenchyma of a patient with diabetes and pyelonephritis: management?
cards.backHtml: Emphysematous pyelonephritis: IV antibiotics plus percutaneous drainage; nephrectomy if no improvement.

cards.frontHtml: Pyelonephritis in pregnancy: setting and drug?
cards.backHtml: Admit; IV beta-lactam such as ceftriaxone; then suppression or culture surveillance until delivery.

cards.frontHtml: Catheter-associated UTI in a catheter in place for more than 2 weeks: what before antibiotics?
cards.backHtml: Remove or replace the catheter and culture urine from the new catheter (never from the bag).
